title: City Lights

title: Beauty and the Beast
review: This is what comes to mind when I think of Beauty and the Beast, rather than the Disney film. The surreal visuals surprised me.

title: The Third Man
review: The direction, visuals and music are still burned into my brain. I'd mistakenly thought until I grew up that Orson Welles directed it.

title: Singin' in the Rain
review: I like the Hollywood musicals of the "good old days", and this is my favorite. When I was a kid, I was in love with this period of America.

title: The Wages of Fear
review: The extreme realism shocked me. It's got its own Mario and Luigi. Yves Montand has great presence.

title: 12 Angry Men
review: This film made me think about just how inaccurate one's assumptions and stereotypes can be. It also was my first exposure to the American jury system.

title: Kanal
review: Most people would probably pick Ashes and Diamonds as their favorite of Wajda's films, but I like this one the best. It had a big influence on MGS, too.

title: The Pink Panther
review: My favorite comedic actor is the late Peter Sellers. I like nearly all of Edwards's and Sellers's films together, though the Pink Panther films are the best. This is where MGS gets its sense of humor.

title: The Umbrellas of Cherbourg
review: A bittersweet film. Catherine Deneuve is cute. This type of love story, where circumstances keep two people apart, really gets to me.

title: Fantastic Voyage
review: This never gets old for me. A popcorn movie, it combines science fiction and espionage to great effect. The art direction and special effects depicting the inner workings of the human body are not only amazing but scientifically accurate as well.

title: Somewhere in Time
review: I adore Richard Matheson's original novel and this movie, which he also wrote. Jane Seymour is really beautiful. I'm a sucker for this type of romance movie. John Barry's music is good, too.

title: Das Boot
review: This is my favorite submarine film. It's a powerful depiction of a group of men in extreme circumstances.

title: Mauvais Sang
review: I really like Carax, and this is my favorite work of his. It's a cool movie.

title: A Better Tomorrow II
review: This is one of my favorite John Woo films, right up there with Hard-Boiled. I still cry every time I watch it.

title: Fantastic Planet
review: The originality of its world and style left me speechless.

title: Wicked City
review: One of Mr. Kawajiri's best works. I respect him very much. It has an unrivaled speed to it! Seeing it now, it's like watching The Matrix.

title: Crayon Shin-chan: The Storm Called: The Adult Empire Strikes Back
review: A tearful, painful yet inspiring film for my generation. Anyone who writes it off as just a kids' movie is making a big mistake. It's an amazing film that a family can enjoy together, laughing, crying, cherishing.

title: Yojimbo
review: One of my favorite Kurosawa films, along with High and Low and Seven Samurai.

title: Asobi
review: This is based on Akiyuki Nosaka's novel. It's not the best of Masumura's films, but I just like it a lot for some reason. I was a fan of Keiko Sekine when I was a kid.

title: Castle of Sand
review: It has incredible direction, and moved and amazed me in ways the book didn't, in ways only film can. Yasushi Akutagawa's music is wonderful, too.

title: Burst City
review: This is Sogo Ishii's greatest work!! It has fantastic energy and soul! Mr. Ishii is my mentor in spirit. When I first saw this I thought, I want to be like him some day!

title: Night and Fog
review: This documentary belongs in my top thirty list. It's based on Viktor Frankl's novel Man's Search for Meaning, which my father made me read as a kid as well.

title: Casablanca
review: I didn't really understand what this was about when I was a kid, but the ending, the music and especially Ingrid Bergman's beauty (my mother was a big fan of her) are forever etched in my memory.

title: The Shadow's Edge
review: Went to see Jackie Chan's 'The Shadow's Edge' first thing this morning!! Holy…this was INSANE!!!! I couldn't get enough!!! Absolutely incredible!!! From the opening shot to the very last moment, it's an all-out feast: action, espionage, pacing, thrills, drama, set pieces and of course 'Jackie,' all packed in. The contrasts are brilliant: analog vs. digital, AI vs. the pursuit team, youth vs. battle-hardened veterans across generations. Highly, highly recommended.

title: Dollhouse
review: I watched Dollhouse on the plane. Wow, it was terrifying. This might be a new masterpiece of Japanese horror. The introduction, structure, and script are all excellent. With no one to rely on, in the end, the characters have no choice but to resolve things themselves. Everything is meticulously planned and thought out until the very end. It doesn't rely on jump scares, but instead uses a slow-burning tension to confront fear. It really nails the key elements of horror.

title: Kokuho
review: This morning, I finally got to see 'Kokuhō (National Treasure).' I haven't read the original novel. The film was very well made. In its cinematography, framing, density, camera work, and visual composition, it strongly evoked a European sensibility, yet what it captured was unmistakably the forbidden world of Kabuki.

title: Suzuki=Bakudan
review: I watched the movie 'Suzuki = Bakudan (Bakudan)' with Mura-shu. I had read the original novel when it was first published, but since it was already like three years ago, I'd forgotten the details. So, I enjoyed it while recalling bits and pieces. As an entertainment film, it's first-class. It was fun.

title: A.I. Artificial Intelligence
review: Tonight, I'm rewatching Steven Spielberg's 'A.I.' (2001) for the first time in 25 years. Hard to believe it was released the same year as MGS2.

title: Togo
review: I was able to finally watch the movie 'Togo' (2019), which I'd been wanting to see for a long time after finding it on a streaming service. In the freezing Alaskan town of Nome, a diphtheria outbreak breaks out. With a blizzard approaching, planes can't be used to transport the serum. To save the critically ill children, musher Leonard (Willem Dafoe) sets out on a brutal, life-or-death journey—nearly 1,000 kilometers round trip—by dog sled, led by his aging dog Togo (12 years old), to retrieve the serum. The film is based on the real 1925 serum run to Nome. It was wonderful. I cried so many times. Dafoe is incredible, and so is the dog who plays Togo. Honestly, this was basically DEATH STRANDING. It even made me want to be connected to a dog by the harness. Highly recommended.

title: Akira
review: I was going to read a book, but found out that the uncut version of 'AKIRA' is on TV tonight, so I decided to watch that—even though I have the 4K UHD.

title: Interstellar
review: Tonight, I'm rewatching 'INTERSTELLAR' (2014) for the first time in 12 years since seeing it in theaters.

title: Contact
review: Last night, rewatching 'Interstellar' made me want to rewatch 'Contact' (1997) again. So tonight, I'm watching this beloved film. We're a generation deeply influenced by Carl Sagan and the SETI program. I've returned to this movie many times over the years. A father and daughter, a journey into the unknown, wormholes, relativity, Lynda Obst, Kip Thorne. 'Interstellar' and this film feel like twins.

title: Cuckoo
review: I'd been waiting a long time for the Japanese theatrical release of 'Cuckoo' (2024), the horror film starring Hunter Schafer, but it suddenly came straight onto Amazon Prime. So I watched it under its Japanese title, 'Kakkō.' The film seems to play on both the slang meaning and the biology of cuckoos, echoing the idea of 'cuckoo's nest.' As this is director Tilman Singer's second feature, and with NEON, it was never going to be straightforward. It turned out to be a very strange film. I went in completely blind, and it felt fresh in the same way those unfamiliar Italian or Spanish horror films I secretly watched on late-night TV as a kid. There were moments I genuinely found scary too. It's an off-beat horror that mixes a wide range of elements and themes. And since one of my favorites, Jessica Henwick makes a brief appearance, I enjoyed it all the more.

title: Caught Stealing
review: Darren's new film has finally been released in Japan, so I went to see Darren Aronofsky's 'Caught Stealing.' Whoa!!! It was insanely good!! I was expecting 'Darren's' usual 'hard-to-hit' pitch and braced myself in the 'batter's box,' but it was completely different. A 'curveball' in a whole new sense! And yet, a dead-center 'strike' aimed straight at entertainment! A laugh-out-loud, 80s-style 'caught-up-in-the-chaos' crime action flick! The protagonist's trauma, the clever use of props, and the placement of foreshadowing were all as brilliant as 'Die Hard.' Plus, every single character was fascinating. Highly recommend! The Japan release was way too late, but just like last year's Shadow's Edge, this is a must-see. This time, Darren's film isn't a 'failed steal'—it's a 'home steal.'

title: Memories
director: Katsuhiro Otomo, Koji Morimoto, Tensai Okamura
review: Tonight, I'll rewatch Katsuhiro Otomo's 'MEMORIES' in 4K ultra HD.

title: Hamnet
review: I watched 'Hamnet' at a screening. In just 126 minutes, it encapsulates all the sorrow, pain, loss, fear, love and joy, healing and hope found in life across all times and cultures. That beautiful final scene has the power to rewrite the history of cinema. It lays bare the miracle of movies. To be able to create something like this, Chloé Zhao must be a witch, or perhaps an angel.

title: Crime 101
review: Watched 'Crime 101,' the film adaptation of a novella by our Don Winslow. It was excellent! Completely satisfying! The balance between thrills, action, drama, character work, and foreshadowing is spot-on, all ultimately converging onto the central spine of the story: Highway 101. It reminded me of the kind of high-quality noir films I loved as a kid. Rather than leaning too heavily on extreme violence, excessive car chases, or nonstop gunplay, the film sustains tension through to the end while deeply exploring where each character is headed. It's not about justice or good and evil, nor about law or ethics. Instead, a sense of 'love' for the characters and an almost chivalric code of 'honor' quietly and satisfyingly come to fruition in the final moments. And it was a real pleasure to see Nick Nolte on screen as well.

title: War Machine
review: After seeing the trailer, I had been curious about Patrick Hughes' 'War Machine.' Tonight I was actually planning to watch 'Xtro,' since I just bought the Blu-ray, but the other film started streaming today, so I decided to watch this one first. Wow, it was quite entertaining. It's basically 'Predator' x 'Metal Gear'! A geek-pleasing film that really evokes the feel of 80s–90s sci-fi action movies. If you like this kind of thing, you should have a great time with it. Alan Ritchson from 'Reacher' ('Jack Reacher: The Outlaw') brings great flavor to the role. Dennis Quaid also appears in it.

title: The Housemaid
review: Watched 'The Housemaid,' 'Tokyo Taxi,' and 'Rental Family' on the flight. I read The Housemaid last year. I was too busy to participate in Hide-mys 2025, but among the mysteries I read last year it easily ranked in my Top 5. The two leads, Sydney Sweeney and Amanda Seyfried, aren't far from how I imagined the characters while reading, so the adaptation works fairly well. If you haven't read the original, I'm sure there will be a moment that makes you go 'Ah!' in surprise.

title: Tokyo Taxi
review: 'Tokyo Taxi' is the Tokyo version of 'Driving Madeleine.' A warm and heartfelt film, very much in the style of director Yoji Yamada. Chieko Baisho was wonderful. But watching it also made me think about my own later years.

title: Rental Family
review: The last film, 'Rental Family,' was quite interesting. Before watching it, I imagined something closer to 'Shoplifters', but the theme and story are completely different. Watching it, I kept thinking: 'Ah… this is Japan.' Japan's scenery, atmosphere, climate, culture, customs, kindness, the way people look at each other, religious sensibilities, human connections. Everything is depicted with great care. The casting of Brendan Fraser creates a wonderful chemistry. A film I hope many people will see.

title: Project Hail Mary
review: The astrophage space scene in 'PROJECT HAIL MARY' was created by tiny LEDs placed on chicken wire that were used while pouring water in front of the lens to refract the light. It was then shot with an Alexa LF camera with the infrared filter removed.

title: The Mandalorian and Grogu
review: I watched 'Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu' in IMAX. Back in 2019, I had only seen the opening of The 'Mandalorian' while examining the LED-shot 'virtual production' technology, but this time I had no problem diving in. Action, car chases, close-quarters combat, sword fights, gun battles, death matches, aerial combat, giant monsters, giant mechs. A complete 'everything versus everything' showcase. CGI, puppets, special makeup, animatronics, stop motion. Even the behind-the-scenes craftsmanship feels like it has everything packed in. X-Wings, AT-ATs, AT-RTs, speeders, stormtroopers, droids. Nearly every element from across the entire history of the Star Wars saga is in as well. An entertainment spectacle made with craftsmanlike skill by Jon Favreau.

title: Supergirl
review: I saw 'Supergirl' in IMAX. It wasn't a 'superhero movie' about saving the Earth through self-sacrifice as 'justice' confronts 'evil.' It was a coming-of-age story about saving oneself, Kara, as she struggles with her own trauma. Structurally, it feels less like 'Mad Max: Fury Road' (2015), where everyone is driven purely by survival instinct beyond notions of good and evil, and more like The Good, the Bad and the Ugly (1966), where heroes, villains, and scoundrels all converge.

title: Backrooms
review: The Backrooms. A world where nostalgia and novelty attack you in the form of 'art.' I'm blown away. It reminds me of pseudo-3D games from the 2D era, back in the dawn of RPGs and the Family Computer (NES), before polygons and textures existed. Simulated 3D spaces built from looping, repetitive visuals: digital labyrinths unconstrained by the rules of architecture. I used to draw maps on graph paper just to keep track of where I was. That sense of confinement. That feeling of anxiety. Both are revived here in live action. The art direction is clever, incorporating elements of art, architecture, and psychology. This is a 21st-century liminal-space version of 'CUBE,' a work of surrealism and cubism in which video games of the 1980s and the modern world connect across dimensions.

title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day
review: Watched 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day.' A lonely hero. A lonely Spidey. A lonely Peter Parker. It felt fresh, and I really enjoyed it. Until now, Spider-Man films have generally been grouped into self-contained trilogies. With each new iteration, the cast and creative team changed, allowing the franchise to reinvent itself for a new era. This time, however, while both the cast and the story continue from the previous film, everything has been reset. The film focuses on Peter, once again alone, and the loneliness and inner conflict that come with that. It can be seen both as the beginning of a new series and as a direct continuation of the last one. A very clever structure.

title: The Odyssey
review: At the David Keighley Theater, I watched Christopher Nolan's 'The Odyssey' (shot entirely with IMAX film cameras) presented in 70mm IMAX film. Rather than simply watching the screen, I felt as though I was there the entire time. It was more than watching it, I witnessed it. The impact was close to what I felt when I was in elementary school and when I first experienced the 'Cinerama' at the 'Osaka OS Theater.' Despite the enormous 1.43:1 screen, Christopher Nolan and Hoyte van Hoytema's cinematography brings us remarkably close to the actors' faces. Through an exceptionally shallow depth of field and elegant pull-focus shots that shift our attention to the finest details, they relentlessly follow the characters' anguish and fate. The cast delivers performances powerful enough to withstand every bit of that extraordinary resolution. Nolan's signature storytelling, with its meticulously interwoven timelines, is very much present here as well. Together, these elements elevate one of the world's best-known classical epics into an intimate, deep human drama. It was magnificent.

title: The Last House
review: I watched 'The Last House.' Isolation? Loneliness? There were parts that felt a little like Death Stranding.

title: The Dog Stars
review: Peter Heller's original novel, 'The Dog Stars' (previously published in Japanese under the title Itsuka Boku ga Kaeru Basho / The Place I'll Return to Someday), has been sitting on my bookshelf for years, unread. Since it's literary fiction rather than science fiction, I went to see the movie picturing it might be something along the lines of Cormac McCarthy's 'The Road.' The music was by Harry. They weren't selling (didn't make) a pamphlet for the film.

title: Heart of the Beast
review: Watched David Ayer's 'Heart of the Beast.' A story about a veteran and a former military reconnaissance dog, both suffering from PTSD, trying to survive and make their way home. The beautiful but unforgiving Alaskan wilderness stands in their way. There's very little dialogue, but you can really feel the strong bond between the two of them (Brad Pitt and the dog). I have to admit, it made me cry. And in the end, the dog's name, 'Odin,' hits you like a body blow. It's a shame they didn't make a program for the film.

title: Resident Evil
review: I wasn't particularly interested at first, but since it's Zach Cregger's latest film, I went to see 'Resident Evil.' Right from the opening, it hits you with music reminiscent of 'The Thing.' From there, it's a relentless barrage of classic horror techniques, terrifying situations, and jump scares that never lets up until the very end. This isn't a film adaptation of 'Resident Evil.' It's a film about the experience of playing 'Resident Evil,' controller in hand. It reminded me of how I felt when I first played the original 'Resident Evil' on PlayStation back in 1996. I was just like Bryan in this movie. I kept getting game over after game over, shouting 'F***!' over and over again. lol

title: Digger
review: I had been holding off on posting my thoughts until the interview was released. Director Iñárritu's 'DIGGER' is a film that all of us living in today's world should see. It is a work that remains with the audience, provoking reflection and sounding alarms. As you absorb this film and carry it with you, a 'tool (a digger)' for delving deeper into the future will surely begin to take shape within you. This is a film that will stay by your side for years to come.

title: Whalefall
review: I watched 'Whalefall.' I had received a copy of Daniel Kraus's novel, on which the film is based, quite some time ago, but hadn't had the chance to read it yet. Kraus was also involved in writing the screenplay. It was a literary film that explored, in a somewhat metafictional way, the Steinbeck-like relationship between whales and humans as part of an ecosystem, alongside the familial bond between father and son. The visual effects were also outstanding. However, I don't think I'll be eating squid for a while. I love whales. They appear frequently in my games. In MGS2, Raiden is swallowed, digested, and excreted by the enormous Arsenal Gear, a whale that swallows digital information. Whales also feature in MGSV and DEATH STRANDING. There are references to Herman Melville's 'Moby-Dick' as well.

title: Godzilla Minus Zero
review: I went to the Japan premiere of 'Godzilla Minus Zero' at TOHO Cinemas Hibiya. As a huge Godzilla fan and a fan of Minami Hamabe, this is a film I've been eagerly waiting three years to see. And I got to see it in IMAX!!! There were moments that played out just as I imagined, moments that surprised me in the best possible way, moments beyond anything I could have imagined, and moments clearly made for hardcore fans (scenes that brought tears to my eyes as a longtime fan, and scenes I'd always dreamed of seeing brought to life). By the final climax, I was so excited that I practically felt dorsal fins sprouting from my back and an atomic heat ray blasting out of my mouth! Once it's released, I'll definitely be seeing it a few more times in IMAX.
